A side-by-side comparison of epigeal and hypogeal germination. Left panel (Epigeal): A cowpea seed germinating. The curved hypocotyl emerges from the soil, pulling two thick green cotyledons above the soil line, with true leaves forming above them. Right panel (Hypogeal): A maize seed germinating. The seed remains below the soil line while a straight shoot (epicotyl) pierces the soil surface and forms leaves. Clean flat textbook illustration, white background.

A four-panel diagram showing vegetative propagation methods. Panel 1 (Cutting): A slanted cassava stem planted in soil with roots and new shoots emerging. Panel 2 (Budding): A T-cut on a rootstock stem with a single bud being inserted and tied tightly with polythene tape. Panel 3 (Grafting): A V-shaped scion stem fitted into a cleft in a rootstock and tied. Panel 4 (Air Layering / Marcotting): A branch on a tree wrapped in a plastic pouch containing moist soil, with small roots visible inside the pouch. Clean flat textbook illustration, white background.

Step-by-step diagram of transplanting. Step 1: A hand trowel lifts a small tomato seedling from a nursery bed, keeping a clump of dark soil (ball of earth) around its roots. Step 2: A field layout showing a hole dug in a ridged bed. Step 3: The seedling is placed carefully into the hole at the same depth as before. Step 4: A watering can with a fine rose sprinkles water on the newly planted seedling. The sun is shown low on the horizon with a label "Late afternoon". Clean flat textbook illustration, white background.
